pos: n. (a man of Judah whose families are named in the genealogies; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Acharchel, of uncertain sense, perhaps brother of Rachel or behind the rampart; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:8.
biblical_def: Aharhel occurs once: “And Coz begat Anub, and Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum” (1 Chronicles 4:8). The verse belongs to the densest genealogical chapter in Scripture, a register of the tribe of Judah running from Pharez outward through branch after branch: “The sons of Judah; Pharez, Hezron, and Carmi, and Hur, and Shobal” (1 Chronicles 4:1). What is remarkable about Aharhel's verse is what stands immediately after it. In the middle of these names, with no preparation and no explanation, the Chronicler stops to tell a story about a man and his prayer, and records that God answered: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10). Then the list resumes as though nothing had happened. Aharhel is a name on one side of that interruption, and the shape of the chapter is itself a doctrine: God keeps the register and God hears the prayers, and the two belong in the same column.

corruption_summary: The prayer of Jabez is detached from its genealogy and sold as a technique for increase, where the man's chief petition was to be kept from evil.
corruption_paragraphs: Two verses out of this chapter have been printed on their own, marketed, and made the basis of a method for obtaining prosperity. The prayer will not bear it. Of its four petitions, the weight falls on the last two — that God's hand might be with him, and that he might be kept from evil so that it would not grieve him — and the first two are asked inside a book about tribal inheritance, where to enlarge a coast is to receive what God has promised, not to acquire what a man has coveted. A petition turned into a technique has been made to mean the reverse of what it says.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the setting. Jabez prays in the middle of a list of names like Coz, Anub, Zobebah, Harum and Aharhel, men of whom nothing else is known; and the Chronicler troubled to write down that God granted his request. The encouragement is for the obscure, which is why it was put where it was.

pos: n. (father of Eliphelet, one of David's thirty; also called Ur, named twice)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achasbai, of uncertain sense; the translators' margin at 1 Chronicles 11:35 gives Ahasbai as an alternative to Ur, so that one man bears both names.
biblical_def: Ahasbai is named as a father in the roll of the thirty: “Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” (2 Samuel 23:34). The Chronicles parallel names the same man's son differently and his father differently again: “Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur” (1 Chronicles 11:35) — and the translators' margin at that verse notes Eliphal as an alternative for Eliphelet and Ur as an alternative for Ahasbai. One man, then, under two names, which is common enough in Israel; this entry covers both and no separate entry is made for Ur. He is called the son of the Maachathite, which places the family on the northern border toward Maachah. The company he belonged to is set out in the surrounding verses: “Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite” (2 Samuel 23:33), and the whole is counted at the end: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). A father named twice, each time under a different name, with nothing recorded of him but that his son stood with David.

corruption_summary: Double names in the parallel rolls are offered as proof of textual confusion, where the translators' own margin shows the two names belong to one man.
corruption_paragraphs: Ahasbai and Ur, Eliphelet and Eliphal, Sharar and Sacar: four names for two men in two verses, and the whole cluster is regularly produced as evidence that the text has broken down. The Authorized Version's margin answers it on the page. The translators noted the alternatives at 1 Chronicles 11:35 precisely because they understood the names to be variants of one another, and they printed both rather than choosing. Men of Scripture commonly bore two names — Jacob and Israel, Simon and Peter, Saul and Paul — and a register is not corrupt for recording the one its own source used.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the one-entity rule is a rule of truth and not of tidiness. Ur and Ahasbai are one man, so he gets one entry and both names are named in it. A reference work that made two men out of two names would be adding to Scripture, not serving it.

pos: n. (a son of Helem in the tribe of Asher; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Amal, labour or toil, from the verb 'amal, to labour or to be wearied; named once as a proper name, 1 Chronicles 7:35.
biblical_def: Amal occurs once as a proper name: “And the sons of his brother Helem; Zophah, and Imna, and Shelesh, and Amal” (1 Chronicles 7:35). He belongs to the register of Asher, which begins a few verses earlier: “The sons of Asher; Imnah, and Isuah, and Ishuai, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:30), and the verse before his names the parallel household: “And the sons of Shamer; Ahi, and Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram” (1 Chronicles 7:34). The tribe's summary is unusually warm for a genealogy: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). The word 'amal is one of the common Hebrew nouns for toil, and it carries through Scripture the whole weight of labour under the sun — Ecclesiastes uses it again and again for work that wearies. A father who named his son Labour was saying something, and the son is counted among the choice and mighty men of a tribe.

corruption_summary: Work is treated either as the whole meaning of a life or as a curse to be escaped, where Scripture makes it a creation ordinance that the fall made toilsome.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet over the word labour. The first makes work the measure of a man, so that identity and worth are earned by output; the second treats work as nothing but the curse, to be minimised and escaped. Scripture holds neither. Adam was set to dress and keep the garden before the fall, so labour is an ordinance of creation and good; the curse added the sweat, the thorns and the weariness that 'amal names. Ecclesiastes faces the weariness honestly and still says a man should eat his bread and rejoice in his labour, for it is the gift of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that toil is real and is not final. A man of Asher was named Labour and is listed among the choice and mighty men of his tribe; and the apostle tells a church that their labour is not in vain in the Lord, which is the only ground on which wearying work can be done with a glad heart.

pos: n. (a Levite in the line of the singers, and an ancestor of a priest; named twice)
etymology: Hebrew 'Amtsi, strong or my strength, from 'amats, to be strong or courageous; named twice, 1 Chronicles 6:46 and Nehemiah 11:12.
biblical_def: Amzi is named twice, and in both places as a link in a Levitical line. The first stands in the genealogy of the house set over the music of the sanctuary: “The son of Amzi, the son of Bani, the son of Shamer” (1 Chronicles 6:46). The purpose of that whole register is given earlier in the chapter: “And these are they whom David set over the service of song in the house of the LORD, after that the ark had rest” (1 Chronicles 6:31), and the register widens to take in the rest of the tribe: “Their brethren also the Levites were appointed unto all manner of service of the tabernacle of the house of God” (1 Chronicles 6:48). The second occurrence is in the roll of those who returned and settled Jerusalem: “And their brethren that did the work of the house were eight hundred twenty and two: and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pelaliah, the son of Amzi, the son of Zechariah, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchiah” (Nehemiah 11:12). Whether one man or two the text does not say, and the dictionary will not decide it. The name means strong, and both bearers of it are men whose whole record is a place in a line that led to someone serving in the house of God.

corruption_summary: Music in worship is treated as a matter of taste, where David appointed it by office, by name and by family under the regulative principle.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern worship practice assumes that music is adiaphora: a question of style, audience and preference. 1 Chronicles 6 describes something quite different. David set men over the service of song by appointment, from named families, in a sanctuary whose furniture and ordinances were all prescribed; the singers were Levites, with a charge as definite as those who carried the vessels. Whatever liberty remains in forms, worship in Scripture is ordered by God and not assembled by the congregation's inclination.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the men who sang were counted and named. A line of nine or ten obscure fathers stands in the Chronicler's register because one descendant held an office in the house of the LORD, and after the captivity the same careful reckoning was done again. God's worship has never been casual about who leads it.

pos: n. (a son of Midian, grandson of Abraham by Keturah; named twice)
etymology: Hebrew 'Abida', my father knows, from 'ab, a father, and yada', to know; named twice, Genesis 25:4 and 1 Chronicles 1:33.
biblical_def: Abida is one of Abraham's grandsons by his second wife: “And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah” (Genesis 25:4), repeated with a variant spelling of one brother in Chronicles: “And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Henoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these are the sons of Keturah” (1 Chronicles 1:33). The marriage is recorded in a single sentence: “Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah” (Genesis 25:1), and what follows the list of her children is the point of the chapter: “And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac” (Genesis 25:5). Abraham had many sons; the covenant ran through one. Midian, Abida's father, gave his name to the people who would later oppress Israel under Gideon and among whom Moses found refuge and a wife. The name Abida means my father knows, which is a good name for a man in a line that received gifts and sent away, while the promise went to the son of the promise.

corruption_summary: Abraham's other sons are produced as evidence that election is arbitrary or unjust, where Scripture presents it as God's free and righteous choice and still blesses the rest.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 25 is uncomfortable reading for a generation that treats equal outcome as the definition of justice. Abraham had Ishmael, and six sons by Keturah, and Isaac; and the covenant went to Isaac alone, with the others sent away with gifts. The apostle takes up exactly this and makes it the ground of the doctrine of election, arguing that the children of the promise are counted for the seed and that God's purpose stands on His own calling and not on birth. That is not injustice; it is the only reason any sinner has hope at all.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's choosing is free and His kindness is wide. Abida's line was not the covenant line and was not cursed; Midian received a land and a history, and a Midianite priest's daughter became Moses' wife. Election is particular; common grace is not.

pos: n. (the third son of Ishmael; named twice)
etymology: Hebrew 'Adbe'el, commonly explained as chastened of God, or a miracle of God; named twice, Genesis 25:13 and 1 Chronicles 1:29.
biblical_def: Adbeel is the third of Ishmael's twelve sons: “And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam” (Genesis 25:13), and Chronicles repeats the order with the other spelling of the firstborn: “These are their generations: The firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; then Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam” (1 Chronicles 1:29). The list closes with a summary that uses a particular word: “These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations” (Genesis 25:16). Twelve princes is the exact term God had used in the promise made to Abraham years before: “And as for Ishmael, I have heard thee: Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly; twelve princes shall he beget, and I will make him a great nation” (Genesis 17:20). Adbeel is thus one-twelfth of a promise kept, named in a register that exists to show the word of God coming true for a son who was not the son of the covenant.

corruption_summary: Ishmael is treated as rejected and cursed, where God promised to bless him and the register records the promise fulfilled to the number.
corruption_paragraphs: Ishmael is commonly handled as the discarded son, and the passages about him are read as a blanket rejection. Scripture is more careful and more generous. God heard Abraham's plea for him, blessed him by name, promised him fruitfulness and twelve princes and a great nation, and then had the twelve written down so the promise could be checked. The covenant of grace ran through Isaac, and that is a distinction Scripture insists upon; but it is not the same thing as a curse, and Genesis 25 is the proof.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is exact in His promises even to those outside the covenant line. He said twelve princes; the list names twelve, by their towns and their castles. A God who counts out a blessing to a son He did not choose for the covenant may be trusted with the promises He has made to those He did.

pos: n. (one of David's thirty, son of Sharar the Hararite; named twice)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achi'am, commonly explained as mother's brother, from 'ach, a brother, and 'em, a mother; named twice, 2 Samuel 23:33 and 1 Chronicles 11:35.
biblical_def: Ahiam is one of the thirty: “Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite” (2 Samuel 23:33). Chronicles gives his father's name in another form: “Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur” (1 Chronicles 11:35), and the translators' margin there notes Sharar as the alternative to Sacar, so one father is meant. The surrounding verses name his fellows: “Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” (2 Samuel 23:34), and the roll closes with its total: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). Hararite marks the family as mountaineers — the word is from the Hebrew for a mountain — and three of the thirty bear it, so one hill country sent a notable share of David's best men. Of Ahiam himself nothing else is told: no deed, no word, no death. He is in the book because he was one of the men who stood with the Lord's anointed, and Scripture thought that worth recording twice.

corruption_summary: A life summed up in one clause is treated as a life of no account, where Scripture records such men by name and God promises to remember the least service.
corruption_paragraphs: An age that measures a life by its visibility finds a man like Ahiam unintelligible: a name, a father, a hill country, and nothing else. But Scripture is full of such entries, and it is the same book that says a cup of cold water given to a disciple shall not lose its reward, and that the Lord's servants will be told well done for faithfulness in little. The register of the thirty is a small anticipation of a larger book, in which names are written that the world never knew.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faithfulness, not fame, is what God records. Ahiam left no deed on the page and is named twice in the word of God. His whole biography is that when David had nothing, he was there.

pos: n. (a son of Dishan the Horite; named twice)
etymology: Hebrew 'Aran, commonly explained as a wild goat, or firm; named twice, Genesis 36:28 and 1 Chronicles 1:42.
biblical_def: Aran is named in the register of the Horites of Seir: “The children of Dishan are these; Uz, and Aran” (Genesis 36:28), and the same pair stands in Chronicles: “The sons of Ezer; Bilhan, and Zavan, and Jakan. The sons of Dishan; Uz, and Aran” (1 Chronicles 1:42). The Horites were the people in the land before Esau's descendants took it: “These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land; Lotan, and Shobal, and Zibeon, and Anah” (Genesis 36:20). Genesis 36 is remarkable for what it is doing. It is a full chapter of Edomite genealogy and a list of Edom's kings, given in the middle of the story of Israel, and it includes the observation that Edom had kings first: “And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel” (Genesis 36:31). The rejected line prospers early and visibly. Aran is a name in it, and the chapter is set in Scripture to teach a patient reader that early prosperity is not the same as the blessing.

corruption_summary: Prosperity is taken as the sign of God's approval, where Genesis 36 shows the rejected line crowned with kings while the chosen line lived in tents.
corruption_paragraphs: The health-and-wealth instinct reads outward success as divine endorsement, and it has to look away from Genesis 36. Esau's line is given dukes, chiefs and a succession of kings, and the Holy Ghost notes that they reigned before Israel had any king at all; meanwhile Jacob's family is a household of shepherds heading for famine and slavery in Egypt. The chapter is placed exactly where it is to make the comparison unavoidable, and the prophet Malachi afterwards sets the whole account in its proper frame.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's favour is not read off a man's circumstances. The Horites and the Edomites after them had the land, the kings and the castles; the promise was with the tent-dwellers. Faith judges by the word and not by the register of titles.

pos: n. (a son of Jether in the tribe of Asher; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ara', of uncertain sense, perhaps lion or gathering; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:38, and distinct from Arah of the next verse.
biblical_def: Ara occurs once: “And the sons of Jether; Jephunneh, and Pispah, and Ara” (1 Chronicles 7:38). He is not to be confused with Arah, who stands in the very next verse in another household: “And the sons of Ulla; Arah, and Haniel, and Rezia” (1 Chronicles 7:39). Two similar names in consecutive verses, belonging to two different men — a reader in haste will merge them, and the Authorized Version keeps them apart because the Hebrew does. The register belongs to Asher, opened some verses before: “The sons of Asher; Imnah, and Isuah, and Ishuai, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:30), and closed with the tribe's character and numbers: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Asher is the tribe Judges indicted for dwelling among the Canaanites, and here it is twenty-six thousand fighting men led by princes. Scripture gives both accounts and does not reconcile them for us.

corruption_summary: Similar names in adjacent verses are merged by careless reading or called duplication by critical reading, where the text distinguishes two men in two households.
corruption_paragraphs: Ara and Arah, one verse apart, invite two mistakes. The careless reader treats them as one man and a spelling slip; the critical reader treats them as a doublet proving the register was clumsily compiled. The verses themselves forbid both: Ara is a son of Jether, Arah is a son of Ulla, and the households are given separately in sequence. A genealogy that carefully distinguishes two near-identical names in consecutive lines is showing precision, not confusion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the discipline of reading closely. Scripture repays attention to a letter, and a reference work owes its readers the same care: two men, two fathers, two entries, and a note in each pointing to the other.

pos: n. (a descendant of Zerubbabel in the royal line; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Arnan, of uncertain sense, perhaps joyful or swift; named once, 1 Chronicles 3:21, in the line of David after the captivity.
biblical_def: Arnan occurs once, in the post-exilic continuation of David's line: “And the sons of Hananiah; Pelatiah, and Jesaiah: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shechaniah” (1 Chronicles 3:21). The chapter has traced the kings from David to the captivity and then keeps going, through Zerubbabel the governor: “And the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei: and the sons of Zerubbabel; Meshullam, and Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister” (1 Chronicles 3:19), and it ends with a generation counted out: “And the sons of Elioenai were, Hodaiah, and Eliashib, and Pelaiah, and Akkub, and Johanan, and Dalaiah, and Anani, seven” (1 Chronicles 3:24). That is the last word of the royal genealogy in the Old Testament. There is no king at the end of it, only a list of names in a province of Persia. Arnan is one of them, and the whole point of the chapter is that the line did not die. When Matthew writes “And Zorobabel begat Abiud” he is picking up a thread the Chronicler had left hanging, and the throne that was empty for five centuries was never vacated.

corruption_summary: The failure of the monarchy is read as the failure of the Davidic promise, where Chronicles keeps the line on the register through five centuries without a throne.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard account of Israel's history treats the end of the monarchy as the end of the Davidic hope, afterwards reinterpreted by the church as a spiritual claim. 1 Chronicles 3 is a deliberate answer written in advance. The Chronicler, composing after the return, carries the royal genealogy straight through the captivity and on past Zerubbabel for several more generations, naming men with no crown and no kingdom. He is recording that the promise of a son to sit on David's throne had a living line attached to it, and he leaves the list open.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's covenant does not depend on visible succession. For five hundred years there was no king in Jerusalem, and there was always an heir; and when the angel told a virgin of Nazareth that her son would have the throne of His father David, the register had been kept all along.
